newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori up in polls though talks stuck.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori up in polls though talks stuck.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori got another boost in new opinion polls on Tuesday showing most Peruvians approved of his management of a five-week-old hostage crisis even though talks to end it were stalled.

For the third time in the last week, an opinion poll showed the president's uncompromising but non-violent stance against Marxist rebels holding 73 hostages in Lima had majority public support. Even Fujimori's own personal standing with Peruvians was improving.
It was an ironic result of a crisis which, when it broke on Dec. 17, looked more like his worst nightmare than an event likely to revive his shrinking popularity.

At the besieged residence of the Japanese ambassador to Peru, where Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels held their hostages for a 35th day on Tuesday, witnesses said a sometimes surreal war of nerves between the rebels and police continued.

Armed special forces police moved closer to the residence, peeped through the gate and ran across in front in a series of unexplained manoeuvres, while some policemen threw rocks into the driveway. The purpose of this was unclear.
Red Cross officials brought in 30 mattresses for the hostages and inspected nearby houses in an apparent bid to find a suitable location for proposed talks.
But the government and the MRTA remained far apart, with the rebels demanding that negotiations include their main demand of freedom for some 400 jailed comrades, and Fujimori rejecting it.
Of 900 Peruvians questioned in the latest survey by Apoyo, a respected polling group, 59 percent thought Fujimori was doing a good job while 30 percent disapproved.

Apoyo, whose director Alfredo Torres was among the early hostages freed by the rebels, added that Fujimori's popularity had crept up during the crisis to 47 percent in January from 45 percent in December.
Another polling firm, Compania Peruana de Investigacion de Mercados, found last week that Fujimori's approval rating had risen to 50.3 percent in January from 44.9 percent in December.
And a survey of 400 people in Lima released Sunday by pollsters Analistas y Consultores found that approval of Fujimori's government rose to 50 percent in January from 43 percent in December.
Since taking office in 1990, the president had held high popularity ratings due to the virtual defeat of communist guerrillas, economic reforms and a strong, personalized leadership style.
But last year his popularity plummeted to its lowest level in five years, mostly because of an economic downturn. The MRTA's action was initially seen as likely to further undermine his standing.
Police on Tuesday helped former hostages recover their cars from the area, in some cases running jump cables to the vehicles' batteries to recharge them.

Five cars and a minivan were removed but several vehicles remained, covered in the accumulated dust of the five weeks since their owners drove them to the residence for a diplomatic reception in honour of Japanese Emperor Akihito.

The rebels initially took about 500 hostages after storming the residence but have released most in what the MRTA called "goodwill gestures." The remaining 73 include Peruvian officials and Japanese businessmen, Fujimori's younger brother, Pedro, and the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors.
